scenario: Today’s infrastructure track keeps returning to the same problem: how to keep training and inference steady when capacity, drafts, and budgets are all moving. Production dispatch can follow capacity refusals without first guessing output length. Whether speculative decoding is actually faster depends on judging draft training, candidate allocation, hidden width, and execution conditions together. Agents can already change their own training and inference stacks, but a local speedup is not the same as an end-to-end gain. Planning for sparse attention has to be cheap enough to be worth doing, and the context need not be reread in full at every step, if the model can tell which block the moment needs. Fairness under an hourly electricity cap cannot be read from aggregate throughput alone, and if activations and gradients are to be quantized more aggressively, bit-widths and communication have to keep accuracy layer by layer.

papers.title: Cap-and-Track: Optimizing LLM Inference Request Dispatch Across Shifting Capacity
papers.authors: Benjamin Novotny, Doug Szeto, Chang Wang, Shicheng Chen, George Zhihua Yuan, Bob Kamma, Michael Ge, John Xin Zhou, Andrea Olgiati
papers.summary: A fixed dispatch rate for language-model inference goes stale as fleets resize and request sizes change. Output length is unknown at admission, and a shared provider pool can also lose capacity. One asynchronous design tracks the current admission ceiling from refusals. A fail-fast check at the saturated resource refuses work, surplus requests sit in durable priority queues, and the dispatcher probes up or backs off from those refusals alone, without predicting output length or retuning a fleet-level rate. In a concurrent same-traffic production A/B, the shaper served a classifier on 43% fewer H100s than a queued, fixed-rate precursor, though lower-priority work waited longer at backfill peaks. In a steady-capacity replay on the real engine, its goodput stayed within 1% of a fixed rate tuned above measured capacity. In its busiest day it handled 1.1 billion requests. ==Dispatch can follow capacity refusals, without first guessing how long an output will be.==
papers.abstract: A fixed dispatch rate for LLM inference becomes stale as serving fleets resize and request sizes change. Generative output length is unknown at admission, and shared provider pools can lose capacity. We present Cap-and-Track, a design for asynchronous inference across provider capacity and internal GPUs. Meta's traffic shaper implements Cap-and-Track for post and live-video understanding. Refusals signal the backend's current admission ceiling. Durable priority queues hold excess work outside execution, including refused requests for retry. Cap is a fail-fast admission check at the saturated resource that refuses work before a long wait. Using only those refusals, the Track dispatcher probes upward and backs off. It follows the ceiling without output-length prediction or a fleet-level rate to retune. In a concurrent same-traffic production A/B, the shaper ran per-replica Cap plus Track. papers.title: FACT: Fixed-Budget Allocation and Cross-Step Training for Speculative Decoding
papers.authors: Hadi Fares, Mayssa Hajj Hassan, Ali Salman, Ammar Mohanna
papers.summary: Speculative decoding speeds up generation by verifying several draft tokens in one pass of the target model, but better draft predictions and longer accepted continuations do not necessarily make generation faster. An experimental framework studies how drafter training, candidate allocation, and execution conditions jointly shape acceptance and latency, using a frozen Llama-3-8B-Instruct target. Backpropagating through predicted-feature rollouts with more weight on early steps raises acceptance by 15% to 24% over uniformly weighted detached training. With a fixed budget and matched widths at each depth, confidence-guided allocation raises the speedup over autoregressive decoding from 1.46× to 2.02× on HumanEval. Even then, changing only host-thread settings can nearly wipe out the speedup while leaving acceptance unchanged. ==Draft training and candidate allocation have to be judged together with the actual execution conditions.==
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model generation by verifying multiple draft tokens in a single target-model pass. However, better draft predictions and longer accepted continuations do not necessarily produce faster generation. To examine this gap, we present FACT (Fixed-Budget Allocation and Cross-Step Training), an experimental framework for studying how drafter training, candidate allocation, and execution conditions jointly affect acceptance and latency. Using a lightweight feature-prediction drafter with a frozen Llama-3-8B-Instruct target under greedy decoding, we first examine how training translates into accepted tokens. Backpropagating through predicted-feature rollouts with greater weight on early steps improves acceptance by 15-24% over uniformly weighted detached training, yet average rollout proxy cross-entropy does not reliably rank drafters by acceptance. papers.title: RSIBench-Infra: Can Agents Optimize Their Own Training and Inference Infrastructure at Production Scale?
papers.authors: Hanlin Wu, Yifei Wang, Zhicheng Cai, Huan-ang Gao, Wei-Ying Ma, Ya-Qin Zhang, Jingjing Liu, Hao Zhou
papers.summary: If an agent is to improve itself, the efficiency of training and inference infrastructure is a practical part of that loop. Existing benchmarks mostly look at a single software layer such as the kernel, and it remains unclear whether agents can deliver end-to-end gains under production workloads. One benchmark offers twenty training and inference tasks across model families and modalities, with deployments of up to thirty-two accelerators. Agents start from runnable official recipes, may change the engine, kernel, and instruction layers, and submit those changes as image layers so the result can be redeployed reproducibly. Independent evaluation then measures end-to-end performance under task-specific quality constraints. Across all task results, 66.2% exceed a validated 1.10× speedup. Current agents can already improve production-scale training and inference, but finding effective strategies and consistently turning local wins into end-to-end gains remains hard. ==Infrastructure optimization has to be judged end to end, not by whether one layer got faster.==
papers.abstract: Improving the efficiency of training and inference infrastructure is a practical component of recursive self-improvement. Existing benchmarks for agent-driven optimization largely focus on individual software layers such as kernel, leaving unclear whether agents can deliver end-to-end performance gains under production workloads. We introduce RSIBench-Infra, a benchmark of 20 training and inference tasks spanning diverse model families and modalities, with deployments of up to 32 accelerators on NVIDIA GPUs and Ascend NPUs. Agents start from runnable baselines derived from official recipes and can modify the software stack across engine, kernel, and instruction levels. An OCI image-layer submission protocol captures these changes for reproducible deployment, while independent evaluation measures end-to-end performance under task-specific quality constraints. papers.score_note: RSIBench-Infra：20 个训练/推理基础设施任务，检验 agent 能否在生产负载下优化自身 infra。

papers.title: LoopCache: Accelerating Long-Context Self-Speculative Decoding for Looped Transformers
papers.authors: Zizhuo Fu, Haochen Huang, Shengxuan Qiu, Linye Wei, Ziyu Tang, Runsheng Wang, Meng Li
papers.summary: Looped Transformers apply a weight-shared block over and over, so a compact model can reach a large effective depth, and each recurrent step keeps its own KV cache. Wave-style self-speculative methods pipeline draft and target tokens across loops in a single step, but they update drafts only at fixed loops and ignore later prediction changes. That wastes work on stale trajectories and loads many loops of KV at once, which inflates memory traffic in long context. One method refines drafts in flight across intermediate loops using output confidence, and it rotates through loop-specific caches so each step’s KV traffic stays in a single loop, while independently retaining caches for a few loop-sensitive shallow layers. In experiments, it is 10.25× faster than WaveFront Decoding and 14.56× faster than LoopSpec on average. ==Long-context self-speculation has to update drafts and fetch KV only for the loop that is actually needed.==
papers.abstract: Looped Transformers achieve large effective depth with compact models by repeatedly applying a weight-shared block across R recurrent steps, each maintaining a loop-specific key-value (KV) cache. To accelerate sequential loop execution, recent wave-style self-speculative methods like WaveFront Decoding (WFD) and LoopSpec pipeline draft and target tokens across loops in a single step. However, they face two critical limitations. First, they draft only at fixed loops and ignore intermediate prediction changes, wasting computation on stale trajectories. Second, batching tokens from different loops loads up to Rx the KV cache per step, severely amplifying memory traffic in long-context scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose LoopCache, an efficient self-speculative decoding framework for long-context Looped Transformers. papers.score_note: LoopCache：加速 Looped Transformer 的长上下文自投机解码，服务侧 KV/解码优化。

papers.title: NarrowSpec: Draft Hidden Width Need Not Match the Target in Speculative Decoding
papers.authors: Alagappan Valliappan, Ankit More, Dheevatsa Mudigere, Jatin Mitra
papers.summary: In speculative decoding, a small draft model proposes tokens and the target verifies them in one pass. Draft models that read the target’s hidden states usually inherit the same hidden width. This work shows that the draft’s whole residual stream can run at half or even a quarter of that width while acceptance is largely preserved. For a draft that borrows the target’s vocabulary projection, the trained output adapter folds into it, and the narrower projection leaves the logits unchanged up to rounding. At one request and temperature zero, narrowing the draft speeds up end-to-end decoding by 1.13× to 1.44× on a GB10. At larger batches the speedup reaches 1.21× on both GPUs, and no narrow draft is slower than full width. ==A draft does not have to match the target’s hidden width just to stay aligned with it.==
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding is widely used to speed up generation in large language models (LLMs), with a small draft model proposing tokens that one forward pass of the target model verifies. Draft models that read the target's hidden states, such as DFlash and EAGLE-3, typically inherit the target's hidden width. We show that the draft's whole residual stream can run at half or a quarter of that width while largely preserving acceptance. For DFlash, which borrows the target's vocabulary projection, the trained output adapter folds into it, giving one narrower projection with logits unchanged up to floating-point rounding. We test two drafter families, DFlash and EAGLE-3, on two targets, Qwen3-8B (NVFP4) and GPT-OSS-20B (MXFP4), in SGLang on a B200 and a DGX Spark (GB10). At batch size 1 and temperature 0, narrowing the draft to half or a quarter width speeds up end-to-end decoding by 1.06-1.12x on B200 and 1.13-1.44x on GB10. The speedup holds at larger batch sizes. papers.title: DexAttention: Distributed Sparse Attention through Rapid Online Planning and Persistent GPU Execution
papers.summary: Sparse attention cuts computation, but distributed execution may still move unnecessary data and pay a substantial cost on every operation. Mask-aware assignment and scheduling can reduce those costs, yet replanning for a dynamic mask has to be cheaper than the execution time it saves. One system co-designs fast online planning with persistent execution: an assigner uses GPU-accelerated, topology-aware clustering to balance compute and cut communication, a light scheduler orders coarse communication and computation, and a persistent kernel on each GPU enforces fine-grained dependencies and dispatches ready work. On a sixteen-GPU cluster across eleven configurations, the geometric-mean end-to-end training speedup is 1.39× over the fastest applicable baseline. For dynamic video attention, including planning, it is 2.11× to 2.37× faster than ring attention. ==Planning for distributed sparse attention has to be cheap enough to be worth doing.==
papers.abstract: Sparse attention reduces computation, but distributed execution may still transfer unnecessary data and incur substantial per-operation overhead. Mask-aware assignment and scheduling can reduce these costs, but replanning for dynamic masks must be cheaper than the execution time it saves. We present DexAttention, a distributed sparse attention system that co-designs fast online planning with persistent execution. Its assigner uses GPU-accelerated, topology-aware clustering to balance computational load and reduce communication. A lightweight greedy scheduler orders coarse communication and computation operations, while a persistent kernel on each GPU enforces fine-grained dependencies and dispatches ready tasks. This division keeps detailed synchronization out of planning while enabling overlap without repeated attention launches. papers.score_note: DexAttention：分布式稀疏注意力与持续 GPU 执行。

papers.title: MoE-Context: Show the Model Only What It Needs
papers.summary: Agents often reread their entire history at every step, which is not how people work: we keep what the moment needs and hold the rest as a short note that can be brought back, without deleting it. One method splits the context into blocks. Before each step, a fast yes-or-no pass decides which blocks the step needs; the rest stay as one-line notes that can be recalled. In the version the authors built, the same model makes the decision and then answers, over a single KV cache, and hidden blocks are masked rather than removed. On a laptop, with Qwen3-1.7B on a synthetic lookup task, showing only the needed block raises accuracy from 93 to 119 of 120, and a masked block is as hidden as a deleted one. The model’s own selection is still the weak part, and simple keyword search picks perfectly on this task. ==The context need not be reread in full at every step, but the model first has to tell which block the moment actually needs.==
papers.abstract: AI agents read their whole history at every step. People do not work like that: we keep what the moment needs and hold the rest as a rough note we can recall. MoE-Context applies this to language models. The context is split into blocks. Before each step a fast yes or no pass decides which blocks the step needs; the rest stay as one-line notes that can be brought back, and nothing is deleted. In the version we build, one model makes this decision and then answers, over a single key-value cache where hidden blocks are masked rather than removed. On a laptop with Qwen3-1.7B and a synthetic lookup task, showing only the needed block raises accuracy from 93 to 119 of 120, and a masked block is as hidden as a deleted one. The model's own picking is the weak part. A supervised linear probe written into spare output rows lifts its accuracy from 80 to 110 of 120, but simple keyword search picks perfectly on this task, and the probe does not transfer to a second task. papers.title: Vanguard: Knowing When to Trust the Draft in Speculative Vision-Language Agents
papers.authors: Hanqi Mao, Jiajun Fan, Ruihan Guo, Shuaike Shen, Ziwen Wang, Hui Ren, Xianrui Zhong, Ge Liu
papers.summary: Vision-language agents that browse websites, operate phones, or act in homes reason before every action, so every step waits on a large model, a latency and cost that get in the way of deployment. Step-level speculation lets a small model draft each step and calls the large model only when a draft is rejected, but the outcome rests on the judge. A judge that reads only the step’s text cannot tell whether that step fits the screen in view. A training-free judge, with the screenshot visible, assigns each candidate step a probability of being right in one forward pass, keeps it if it clears a threshold, and otherwise lets the large model write the step. On one Mind2Web test set, a 2B draft screened by this judge reaches 66.5% step success, above the 8B target alone at 64.4%. On the other test set the figures are 66.8% and 63.3%. The large model writes only a minority of the steps, and far more closed-loop episodes are completed. ==Step-level speculation works only if the judge can look at the screen and decide whether the draft can be trusted.==
papers.abstract: Vision-language agents that browse websites, operate phones and act in homes reason before every action, so every step waits for a large model, a latency and cost that stand in the way of deployment. Step-level speculation lets a small model draft each step and calls the large model only on rejected drafts, but its outcome rests on the judge, and a judge that reads only a step's text cannot tell whether the step fits the screen it acts on. We find that a few samples of a small model can contain a correct step about as often as the large model gets the step right, and not always on the same steps: checked against the screen, small drafts can be not only cheaper but better. papers.title: eFAIR: Fair LLM Serving under Hourly Electricity Commitments
papers.authors: You Peng, Youhe Jiang, Chen Wang, Binhang Yuan
papers.summary: Datacenters can buy electricity in day-ahead markets by committing to an amount for each hour. If a language-model service runs inside those hourly budgets, raising aggregate throughput alone can still leave some requests waiting, or much slower than desired. Fair serving has to improve service for the worst-served requests and still reserve electricity for later arrivals whose timing and demand are unknown. The paper compares requests by normalized throughput: a request’s actual output rate divided by the product of its standalone throughput and its service entitlement, and under the hourly electricity constraint it prioritizes the requests with the lowest ratio. The scheduler aligns dispatch, budget allocation, and GPU frequency selection to a shared normalized-throughput target. On H20 and H200 configurations with thirty-two replicas each, the tenth percentile of normalized throughput rises 28.0% to 31.0% over the best budget-feasible baseline, while absolute deviations from the hourly commitment stay below 0.26%. ==Under an hourly electricity cap, fairness cannot be read from aggregate throughput alone.==
papers.abstract: Datacenters can procure electricity in day-ahead markets by committing to energy purchases for individual hours. For LLM services operating within these hourly budgets, maximizing aggregate throughput alone may still leave individual requests waiting or receiving much slower service than desired. Fair serving therefore requires improving service for poorly served requests while reserving electricity for later arrivals whose timing and demand are unknown. To compare service across requests, we define normalized throughput as each request's actual output rate divided by the product of its standalone throughput and its service entitlement, a positive weight representing its desired service level. Using this measure, we formulate fair serving as leximin optimization under an hourly electricity constraint, prioritizing requests with the lowest normalized throughput. papers.score_note: eFAIR：小时级电力约束下的公平 LLM serving。

papers.title: AGoQ: Activation and Gradient Quantization for Memory-Efficient Distributed Training of LLMs
papers.authors: WenXiang Lin, Juntao Huang, LuHan Zhang, Laiyi Li, Xiang Bao, mengyang zhang, Bing Wang, Shaohuai Shi
papers.summary: Cutting the GPU memory needed to train large language models often depends on quantization, but current methods struggle with near-four-bit activations and eight-bit gradients, and often slow convergence or lose accuracy. One method allocates activation bit-widths by layer type and pipeline stage so activation storage is close to four bits, stores gradients in eight bits, and uses an accuracy-preserving eight-bit All-Reduce to shorten communication. On two GPU clusters of up to sixty-four GPUs, with LLaMA models from 8B to 32B, memory falls by up to 52%. Training speed rises by up to 1.34× compared with systems such as Megatron-LM, COAT, and DeepSpeed, while pretraining loss still converges and downstream accuracy stays comparable. ==If activations and gradients are to be quantized more aggressively, bit-widths have to be set per layer, and communication has to keep accuracy at that low width.==
papers.abstract: Quantization is a key method for reducing the GPU memory requirement of training large language models (LLMs). Yet, current approaches are ineffective for 4-bit activations and 8-bit gradients, which would easily cause slow convergence or accuracy loss.
